newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-EMU talks on TARGET at stalemate.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-EMU talks on TARGET at stalemate.

text.p: Negotiations over access to the planned payments system for a single European currency are at stalemate, with countries outside the launch of monetary union set to face even stiffer restrictions than initially feared.

European monetary sources say public debate about TARGET, the cross-border settlement system for the euro, is so acrimonious there is little chance of a compromise between EMU "ins" and "outs" before the European Central Bank (ECB) is formed in 1998.
"A miracle is always possible and discussions continue but I think the positions are too wide apart for a solution to be found," one source told Reuters.
"Initially it was envisaged as not impossible that conditions (access to TARGET) be the same for both sides but the positions have become much more radical since then," he said.

If the impasse lasts, only countries launching the euro in January 1999 will be able to decide who can borrow or lend funds denominated in the new currency during the trading day, allowing instant, risk-free settlement for large-value payments. This is known as intra-day credit.

In theory, banks in all EU countries will be able to access TARGET for payments. But without the intra-day credit facility, they must hold a credit balance covering the amount with their own central bank.

If access to this facility is denied or restricted, banks may not get needed funds as quickly or as cheaply as EMU competitors. Alternatives will be available but bankers say they may not be as efficient.
ARGUMENTS FOR AND AGAINST

Since the row over TARGET broke out in August, banks in Germany and France -- the main political engines of monetary union -- have made clear they do not favour equal credit treatment for "ins" and "outs".

The Bundesbank has taken pains to point out it fears granting credit to countries outside EMU will disrupt the ECB's attempts to control monetary policy because it would boosting liquidity and money supply outside its area of direct control.
"It is not just or sensible to treat unlikes alike," Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said last month.

"A central bank which does not take part in the currency union and thus retains monetary policy sovereignty for its own national currency, cannot create liquidity in euros from nothing," he told a political forum in Bonn.
The Bank of England (BOE) argues that wider use of TARGET will enhance use of the single currency and ensure its success.
It also says euro liquidity would be affected only if intraday credit spilled over into overnight funding -- which could be prevented by stiff interest rate penalties.
"No other measures are necessary or could be justified on monetary policy grounds," the BOE said in a report in September.

"Any attempts to introduce differential terms for "outs" compared to "ins" would be discriminatory and be likely to cotravene both single market legislation and the EU competition law," the report said.
But other likely "in" bankers say it would be grossly unfair for countries outside EMU to reap the benefits of a single currency while escaping the responsibilities.

This would probably include keeping minimum reserve requirements at the ECB in deposits yielding no or little interest, and possibly more expensive access to TARGET if common pricing is enforced only within the EMU block itself.
ALTERNATIVES TO TARGET
The BOE has pledged to smoothe over inconveniences for banks in London, the world's biggest financial centre.
"When it comes to it banks will be able to make payments one way or another -- if there's going to be a problem we will try to find a way around it," a BOE spokesman told Reuters.

If need be, the BOE would take on additional exchange rate risk and hedge it to provide euros for London-based banks, banking sources say. But the costs would probably have to be passed on, which could make this route unappealing.
Other routes for "out" banks in any country would include receiving payments through a subsidiary, branch or correspondent bank based in an EMU state which had access to TARGET there.
Another way would be via what is now the ECU clearing system, which is being upgraded by the Paris-based ECU Banking Association (EBA) to become its future euro payment system.

EBA President Gilbert Lichter told Reuters some details of the plan still had to be worked out. Firstly, a decision on what collateral was needed to ensure settlement had not been resolved with the European Monetary Institute, forerunnner of the ECB.

Secondly, there would be no problem during the day for any member of the EBA. But at the close of trade, any positive or negative balance would have to be settled with the ECB through TARGET and the bank's account at its own central bank.

"A priori it seems difficult to imagine how a bank that does not have an account with an EU central bank can participate in our system because if it did not it would have to ensure it had a balance of nought at the end of the day," he said.
Bankers say the thorny issue which has yet to be settled before they can see whether the alternatives to TARGET are really viable is the pricing of access to the system.

Put simply, TARGET as a whole will comprise the national RTGS (real time gross settlement) systems for large-value financial trades in each EU member state, plus an interlinking network which will join them together.
The problem is that RTGS is a fairly new concept -- it was only introduced to London last April -- and each country's system has to be made compatible with the linking component.

Some countries are building entirely new RTGS systems to comply. Consequently, costs for use of each domestic system differ widely and countries with a cheap, efficient network could underprice their component to attract more business.
The Bank of England says it wants common pricing to extend only to the interlinking component of TARGET, leaving the rest of the charge to differ reflecting costs of national systems.
Understandably, EMU "ins" wants the common charge to cover the whole of TARGET to create a level playing field.
EUROPEAN BANKS ALSO WORRIED
If Britain opts out of EMU, London looks vulnerable but banks in other "out" countries may be hit even harder.
"For the city as a whole, it probably doesn't amount to much although it would be a nuisance for any clearing bank," said Graham Bishop, European financial affairs advisor for Salomon Brothers.
"The ones who could be most damaged could be banks outside of Britain who lose a singificant part of commercial business."
In recent weeks, howls of protest have been heard from banks in both Denmark and Sweden, who are clearly worried that payments business will migrate to their European counterparts.

"What is at stake is potential conflicts between the EU's member states and their respective financial systems, entirely contrary to the overriding purpose of the European process," Sweden's central Bank governor Urban Backstrom said last week.
Switzerland, which is not even a member of the European Union -- has also complained of unfair discrimination.
"A war among financial centres within the EU is not to be ruled out," Jean-Pierre Roth, vice-President of the Swiss National Bank said in October.
